title: Companies Act, 2013 — Sections 12–14 (Registered Office; Alteration of Memorandum and Articles)

content.overview: Sections 12–14 together cover the registered office (s. 12), alteration of the memorandum (s. 13), and alteration of the articles (s. 14). Alteration of objects, name, and registered-office State, and the residual role of the ultra vires doctrine, are central exam themes.
content.glance: Link registered office (s. 12) to alteration of memorandum (s. 13) and articles (s. 14); state the special-resolution and approval routes; note the modern limits of ultra vires.
content.study: Section 12 fixes the registered office and its change. Section 13 regulates alteration of the memorandum: name change, object change, and change of registered-office State, typically by special resolution, with prescribed approvals and filing of the altered memorandum. Section 14 regulates alteration of articles by special resolution, subject to the Act and the memorandum. The classical ultra vires doctrine has been substantially narrowed by modern objects drafting and statutory alteration powers, but acts still beyond the company’s capacity remain vulnerable. Current-law framing: ground each issue in the specific section and the approval route.

sections.heading: Registered Office (s. 12)
sections.body: Duty to maintain a registered office; verification; display; change procedure including State change.

sections.heading: Alteration of Memorandum (s. 13)
sections.body: Name, objects, and registered-office State may be altered by special resolution and prescribed approvals; altered memorandum must be filed.

sections.heading: Alteration of Articles (s. 14)
sections.body: Articles may be altered by special resolution subject to the Act and memorandum; entrenchment has extra safeguards.

sections.heading: Ultra Vires in Modern Context
sections.body: Objects define capacity; statutory alteration powers reduce rigidity; acts still beyond capacity remain challengeable.

examples.title: Object alteration
examples.body: A company passes a special resolution to alter its objects and files the altered memorandum under s. 13. The alteration is effective on compliance with the statutory route.

examples.title: Article conflicting with memorandum
examples.body: An altered article conflicts with the memorandum. The memorandum prevails; s. 14 alteration cannot override the memorandum.

hypotheticals.question: Can objects be altered freely by ordinary resolution?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 13 requires a special resolution and, where prescribed, further approvals and filing.

hypotheticals.question: Does ultra vires still matter after liberal object clauses?
hypotheticals.analysis: Its practical scope is reduced, but acts beyond the company’s capacity as defined by the memorandum and Act remain legally significant.

distinctions.title: Alteration of memorandum (s. 13) vs articles (s. 14)
distinctions.left: Charter change: name, objects, State of office

rows.right: Special resolution subject to Act and memo

misconceptions.trap: Articles can always override the memorandum after alteration.
misconceptions.correction: Articles remain subject to the Act and the memorandum.
Statutory alteration powers and broad objects reduce its reach, but capacity limits still exist.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a ss. 12–14 problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify whether the issue is office, memo alteration, or articles alteration. II. Apply the correct section and approval route. III. Address ultra vires only if capacity is in issue. IV. Conclude.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Correct section; resolution type; approvals; filing; capacity/ultra vires if raised; precise relief.

examTips: Map the issue to s. 12, 13 or 14.
State special resolution and approval requirements.
Treat ultra vires carefully in modern law.
